lesson.title: Clients: The End Systems That Ask First
lesson.summary: Defines the client as the end system that initiates a request to a server, completing the client server pattern and contrasting client behavior with server behavior.
lesson.body:
If a server is an end system that waits to be asked, a client is the end system that does the asking. A client initiates communication: it sends a request to a server and then waits for that server to respond. Your web browser is a client when it asks a website's server for a page. Your email app is a client when it asks a mail server for new messages. A weather app on your phone is a client when it asks a weather service's server for the current forecast. In every case, the client starts the conversation.

This initiating role has practical consequences that mirror, in reverse, the consequences of being a server. A client does not need a stable, well-known address that the rest of the world can find in advance, because nobody needs to locate a client ahead of time, the client is the one doing the locating. This is part of why your laptop or phone can move between networks, get a different address from one WiFi network to the next, or go offline entirely, without breaking the internet for anyone else. Clients also do not need to run continuously. Your phone can be off overnight and simply start fresh conversations with servers whenever it turns back on and wants something.

The client server model built from these two roles, one end system that waits and one that asks, is the dominant pattern for organizing traffic across the internet today. Web browsing, email, video streaming, and most mobile apps all follow it: an app on your device acts as a client, reaching out to a company's servers to request pages, videos, or data. It is worth noting that the roles are not permanent properties of a device, they describe behavior in a given exchange. The same laptop that acts as a client when browsing the web could, if it ran server software, also act as a server for some other application. Many peer to peer applications even have every participating end system act as both a client and a server at different moments, requesting data from some peers while serving data to others.

Clients also vastly outnumber servers in most networks, which is a direct consequence of the roles each one plays. A single popular server might be answering requests from millions of clients over the course of a day, while each of those clients typically talks to only a handful of servers at any given time. This asymmetry is part of why servers are engineered for heavy, sustained load and stable addressing, while clients are engineered for mobility, convenience, and the flexibility to start and stop conversations freely whenever the person using them wants something.

Consider a worked example that ties clients and servers together. You open your phone and tap an app to check today's weather. Your phone, acting as the client, sends a request to the weather company's server. That server, which has been running continuously and listening for exactly this kind of request, looks up the current conditions and sends the forecast back. Your phone receives the response and displays it. The entire exchange only works because the two end systems played complementary roles: one asked, and one was ready to answer.
